case_info.scenario: A 39-year-old female patient with alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma and bone metastases presented in April 2020 with lower back pain, which was aggravated while standing and walking. She reported no known trauma, and no motor or sensory deficits were noted during clinical examination. She had no fever. After the initial sarcoma diagnosis in September 2018, the patient received 8 cycles of doxorubicin hydrochloride and ifosfamide along with regional hyperthermia, followed by good tumor response. The patient had a history of a pathological fracture of L4, which had been treated with radiotherapy and vertebroplasty in November 2019 and remained unchanged on imaging obtained in April 2020. The treatment regimen recently had been switched to gemcitabine hydrochloride and docetaxel in January 2020 following osseous progression during maintenance chemotherapy with trofosfamide, idarubicin hydrochloride, and etoposide. On restaging computed tomography, symmetrical enlargement of both psoas muscles was observed with intramuscular hypodensity (Figure, A). The patient reported lower back pain but no motor or sensory deficits. Further workup with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed extensive, nearly symmetrical swelling in both psoas muscles and sharply delineated, peripheral contrast enhancement of the fascia with strict horizontal bounds (Figure, B and C).
case_info.caption: A, Computed tomography scan showing symmetrical enlargement of both psoas muscles (arrowheads). B and C, Magnetic resonance images showing edema in both psoas muscles and peripheral contrast enhancement of the fascia, with arrowheads pointing to the imaging abnormalities.
case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

dialogue_history.text: I disagree. The symmetrical, bilateral psoas enlargement with peripheral fascial enhancement and strict horizontal bounds is not typical for metastatic extension. This pattern is highly suggestive of a non-malignant inflammatory process, such as psoas abscess or necrotizing fasciitis, which requires urgent diagnostic confirmation. Given the patient's pain and risk of sepsis, immediate MRI with contrast or CT-guided aspiration should be prioritized over assuming disease progression.

4 = High workload

* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

case_info.explanation: Radiation recall is a rare diagnosis in which inflammatory reactions are induced by chemotherapeutic agents in previously irradiated tissues. D’Angio et al1were the first to describe this phenomenon in 1959. In pediatric and adult patients treated first with radiotherapy and then with intravenous administration of actinomycin D, development of erythema was observed and was sharply limited to prior irradiation fields in the course of actinomycin D treatment. Since publication of the study by D’Angio et al,1many cytotoxic agents have been identified as potential triggers for radiation recall events. Among the most frequent drugs associated with these events are anthracyclines and taxanes, such as docetaxel.2In recent years, gemcitabine also was implicated in several cases.3Although radiation recall was initially and most often reported to affect the skin, such reactions associated with use of gemcitabine predominantly seem to be associated with inflammation of internal tissues, especially muscles, triggering radiation recall myositis.4-6 Radiation recall events typically occur days to weeks after the initiation of chemotherapy but have been reported up to 15 years after radiotherapy treatment.7The underlying mechanisms of these events have not yet been elucidated. Distinct mechanisms of action have been proposed because various cytotoxic agents have been associated with this adverse event. These mechanisms include alterations of pharmacodynamics based on abnormal intracellular expression and activity of proteins attributable to radiotherapy-induced injury of exposed tissues and idiosyncratic drug hypersensitivity reactions.2 No strict treatment recommendations for radiation recall myositis are available.6Corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can alleviate symptoms, and discontinuation of the chemotherapeutic agent may be considered depending on clinical severity.8 The patient in this study developed radiation recall myositis triggered by docetaxel and gemcitabine hydrochloride, 2 agents associated with this adverse effect. This condition occurred 5 months after the last course of radiotherapy (total dose: 40 Gy for L4 and 35 Gy for the left tenth rib; ray type: 10 MeV; radiotherapy technique: volumetric modulated arc therapy) and 2 months after commencement of chemotherapy. Besides myositis of both psoas muscles (Figure), the autochthonous back muscles and the intercostal muscles around the left tenth rib, which previously had also been irradiated, also showed signs of myositis on MRI. The extent of myositis reached beyond the 50% isodose line of the radiotherapy plans. There was no diffusion restriction of these lesions observed on MRI, and together with nonelevated C-reactive protein and the absence of fever in the patient, an infectious cause seemed unlikely. Docetaxel and gemcitabine treatments were discontinued, and the patient began taking high-dose prednisone, followed by rapid elimination of the lower back pain. The diagnosis of radiation recall myositis can be challenging if the medical history and treatment timelines are not available in sufficient detail. Characteristic imaging findings may help in identifying a diagnosis, yet they have to be put into context of the patient’s history. Normal inflammatory markers in the blood and the absence of imaging signs of abscess or hematoma help in narrowing down the diagnosis. In the literature, no specific relationship between radiotherapy dose and occurrence of recall myositis has been established. Moreover, no typical temporal association has been identified so far. Oncologists, radiation oncologists, and imaging specialists should be aware of radiation recall myositis to differentiate it from other causes and to ensure timely management of this adverse effect.

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 39-year-old female patient with alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma and bone metastases presented in April 2020 with lower back pain, which was aggravated while standing and walking. She reported no known trauma, and no motor or sensory deficits were noted during clinical examination. She had no fever. After the initial sarcoma diagnosis in September 2018, the patient received 8 cycles of doxorubicin hydrochloride and ifosfamide along with regional hyperthermia, followed by good tumor response. The patient had a history of a pathological fracture of L4, which had been treated with radiotherapy and vertebroplasty in November 2019 and remained unchanged on imaging obtained in April 2020. The treatment regimen recently had been switched to gemcitabine hydrochloride and docetaxel in January 2020 following osseous progression during maintenance chemotherapy with trofosfamide, idarubicin hydrochloride, and etoposide. On restaging computed tomography, symmetrical enlargement of both psoas muscles was observed with intramuscular hypodensity (Figure, A). The patient reported lower back pain but no motor or sensory deficits. Further workup with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed extensive, nearly symmetrical swelling in both psoas muscles and sharply delineated, peripheral contrast enhancement of the fascia with strict horizontal bounds (Figure, B and C).
